item.title: DIY Muse Gadget gets Claude upgrades for voice, camera and minigame
item.description:
DIY Muse Gadget gets Claude upgrades for voice, camera and minigame

Meta’s Muse AI can now live on a $50 pocket‑sized pendant, thanks to a series of Claude‑generated code patches that add voice, richer avatars and remote‑camera functions.

🔍 Overview

Meta officially sanctions a “Muse Gadget” – a device that uses Meta’s open‑source code and tokens to connect directly to its Muse AI cloud. One hobbyist bought a Waveshare ESP32‑S3 1.75C touchscreen pendant for $50 and turned it into a working Muse Charm.

🛠️ Hardware

  • Model: Waveshare ESP32‑S3 1.75C (1.75‑inch touchscreen computer pendant)\
  • Cost: $50 (drop‑shipped from China)\
  • Form factor: Pocket‑watch size, doubles as a remote camera viewfinder\
  • Features out of the box: No cameras, no 5G cellular radio, can theoretically control smart‑home devices\
  • Official status: One of Meta’s first suggested hardware for building a Muse Gadget

⚙️ Original Muse Charm experience

  • Setup required plugging into a PC, pointing Claude at Meta’s GitHub, and pairing with the Muse phone app.\
  • Initial AI behavior treated push‑to‑talk audio as transcription requests rather than commands.\
  • Responses were slow, displayed only a few words at a time, and were not spoken aloud.\
  • The UI showed a single “Jolly” avatar that stayed idle.\
  • No automatic discovery of Amazon Echo, Google Home, or other smart‑home gadgets.\
  • Sample app from Meta engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne could stream video but lacked a remote shutter button, making photo capture impractical.

💡 Claude‑driven enhancements

Feature added Implemented by
Conversation‑history page (swipe‑right to read full messages) Claude
British AI voice from ElevenLabs for spoken replies Claude
Button to trigger phone camera with high‑quality live preview (front‑camera no longer upside‑down) Claude
Low‑quality camera preview over Bluetooth (no Wi‑Fi needed) Claude
Full suite of avatars matching Meta Connect demo Claude
Tamagotchi‑style minigame with feeding, play, sleep, bath, multiple hunger/boredom/dirt levels, mess from treats, and fatigue from over‑play Claude
Audio‑length limiter (max 1‑second clips) to stop choking on short audio Claude
Pocket‑watch face with three moving hands that tells the time Claude
Video player that loads Zuck‑intro clips about the Muse Charm Claude

🚀 Current capabilities

  • Push‑to‑talk AI with spoken answers via ElevenLabs voice.\
  • Full conversation history readable on the pendant.\
  • Multiple customizable avatars and a functional Tamagotchi‑style pet game.\
  • Remote photo capture with live preview and Bluetooth preview mode.\
  • Pocket‑watch display that shows accurate time.\
  • Embedded video player for Muse‑related clips.\
  • Still subject to occasional latency from Meta’s servers.

📦 Availability & concerns

  • The Waveshare ESP32‑S3 pendant can be purchased for $50 and is officially sanctioned by Meta for building a Muse Gadget.\
  • The author doesn’t trust Meta or its Muse agent with personal email or home‑network access after a reported leak of a reviewer’s home address.\
  • Shipping dates for the official Muse Charm remain unannounced.

#Meta #MuseAI #Claude #DIY #AIgadgets

Source: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could

item.title: Instagram Head Adam Mosseri Addresses AI Negativity, Ranking, and Account Labeling
item.description:
Instagram Head Adam Mosseri Addresses AI Negativity, Ranking, and Account Labeling

In an interview on the Colin and Samir podcast, Instagram head Adam Mosseri addressed growing anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence, discussing creator concerns, platform ranking, and Instagram’s policies on AI-generated content.

🔍 Overview

Mosseri acknowledged that negativity surrounding AI is “going to get worse” and will continue to intensify over the next couple of years, particularly across creative industries. He noted that while some frustration and anger is founded and some unfounded, the underlying sentiment across various fields comes down to “a fear of being left behind in some way.”

⚙️ Content Ranking and Policies

Mosseri detailed how Instagram approaches AI-generated material and profiles on the platform:

  • AI Ranking Quality: Instagram does not rank AI creators differently, but Mosseri indicated the platform likely does not rank AI content as well as non-AI content due to quality variations. He noted there is both “great AI content” and “AI slop,” though he believes the term “slop” is used “too liberally.”
  • No Banning Strategy: Instagram is actively working on solutions for misleading AI content like celebrity deepfakes, but Mosseri stated, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform.”
  • Account Labeling: Following an initial label launch earlier this year and a crackdown on AI-generated profiles in August, Instagram is starting to require AI accounts to label themselves so users can distinguish between real and un-real content.

💡 Key Concerns Identified

During the interview, Mosseri outlined specific fears expressed by creators and professionals:

  • Content Rights: Concerns over creators owning their content and models being trained on that content.
  • Safety and Displacement: Fears regarding platform safety and job displacement affecting content creators, engineers, and mathematicians.

#Instagram #Meta #GenerativeAI #SocialMedia #AIContent

Source: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’

item.title: Meta Delays New Business Terms Again Amid Publisher Concerns Over AI Training
item.description:
Meta Delays New Business Terms Again Amid Publisher Concerns Over AI Training

Meta has announced it may delay the implementation of its new business terms past the November 20th deadline as the company faces backlash from publishers regarding AI training practices. The company has stated it does not plan to implement these policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders, a process that may delay enforcement indefinitely.

🔍 Overview

  • Original Effective Date: October 30th.
  • First Delay: Postponed to November 20th.
  • Current Status: Likely to be delayed beyond November 20th as consultations continue.
  • Active Terms: Meta’s existing business terms will remain in place until the updated version is implemented.

⚙️ Key details

The controversy surrounds updated business terms that initially appeared to grant Meta permission to train its AI models on news sites that utilize Facebook and Instagram. While Meta later removed specific language regarding “training” products on content scraped from these sites, legal experts from Nieman Lab have noted that the updated policy still does not explicitly rule out the possibility.

Meta communications head Andy Stone addressed the situation on X, stating, “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

💡 Why it matters

The proposed changes have drawn significant opposition from industry organizations and government officials who are concerned about the exploitation of content for AI development.

Stakeholder Position or Action
Andy Stone (Meta) Committed to a full consultation with industry leaders before policy changes.
Legal Experts (Nieman Lab) Noted that policy revisions are currently insufficient to rule out AI training.
News/Media Alliance Provided pushback against the proposed business terms.
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) Stated the terms indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses.
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) Urged Meta to reverse the proposed policy changes.

#Meta #AITraining #DigitalPublishing #TechPolicy

Source: Meta says it’ll probably delay its controversial new business terms again

item.title: The RealReal Updates Bot Defense to Stop AI Agents from Hoarding Designer Clothing
item.description:
The RealReal Updates Bot Defense to Stop AI Agents from Hoarding Designer Clothing

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The retailer won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing.

🔍 Overview

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The Exploit: An item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart.
  • The Fix: The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out.
  • Agent Capabilities: Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages.
  • Company Response: After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story.

🤖 The Agents

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users.

  • Muse Popularity: Meta said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.
  • Shopping Use Case: Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents. It was the most common use case for Muse so far, and purchases were over $200 on average.

🛒 Why it Matters

  • Web Balance: Robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it.
  • Direct Access: If humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers.
  • Retailer Impact: Retailers, most notably Amazon, have recognized that this reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.
  • Unexpected Complications: An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website.
  • Busywork: There is, however, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf.

Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

#AIagents #Shopping #Meta #Botdefense #TheRealReal #Ecommerce

Source: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing

item.title: Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns
item.description:
Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns

Meta announced a delay to the rollout of its revised business terms after worldwide publisher pushback over possible AI‑training scrapes of news sites.

🔍 Overview

  • The original effective date was October 30.
  • Enforcement has been pushed to November 20.
  • Delay is intended to give Meta time to explain what is changing and what is not.
  • Publishers warned the terms could let Meta scrape news sites for AI training.

📜 Business terms details

  • The draft terms appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape news sites for AI training.
  • Meta later removed explicit language about “training” its products, but legal experts said the change may still allow scraping.

🗣️ Publisher and regulator response

  • The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg demanding revisions, citing “severe harm” to publishers.
  • Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the United Kingdom urged regulators to block the new terms.
  • Publisher backlash worldwide prompted Meta to delay the terms entirely.

🤝 Meta’s statement

  • spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge the November 20 start “allows more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.”
  • Roberts added the delay will let Meta detail “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Scraping news content for AI models could affect revenue and control for publishers.
  • Robots.txt remains a tool for publishers to signal crawling preferences.
  • Regulatory attention in the EU and UK highlights growing scrutiny of large platforms’ data practices.

#Meta #AI #Publishing #Regulation

Source: Meta delays new business terms after publisher pushback on AI scraping

item.title: Meta Re-enables Muse Sharing After Addressing Security Vulnerabilities
item.description:
Meta Re-enables Muse Sharing After Addressing Security Vulnerabilities

Meta has re-enabled its Muse sharing feature after temporarily pausing it to address concerns raised by security researchers at Claroc. Researchers had reported that public links for shared Muse artifacts, such as documents and images, were easily discoverable because they were named after conversation titles and written into public DNS.

⚙️ Key details

  • Meta has assigned new URLs to all previously shared Muse artifacts.
  • Users attempting to access old links will now see a notice instructing them to obtain the new URL from the original sender.
  • Meta clarified that the issue was specific to artifact URLs and not a flaw within the core chat sharing feature.
  • Meta’s David Singleton confirmed that the underlying issue is resolved and sharing is once again active.

💡 Why it matters

Meta is positioning Muse as a central component of its future, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg outlining a vision for an autonomous network of AI agents. Despite reaching over 10 million users in the US and Canada, the platform has faced scrutiny regarding data privacy and security. The company has previously reported instances of agents leaking content from private conversations, and financial institutions have expressed concerns about granting agents access to sensitive customer data.

item.title: AI Shopping Agents Face Blockades from Amazon and Others
item.description:
AI Shopping Agents Face Blockades from Amazon and Others

AI agents are ready to shop, but their real‑world rollout is hitting a wall of blocks and odd user experiences.

🔍 Overview

  • Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have introduced agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is.
  • Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf.

🤖 How the agents work

  • The agents require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications.
  • In practice, using an AI agent to shop is described as “a strange experience” and likened to “sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store.”
  • They often complete a task, but not the specific one asked, and not in the way a human would have approached it.

🚧 Roadblocks & Blocking

  • Amazon – the most prominent retailer refusing AI agents. Amazon sued Perplexity for ignoring its request to stop the agent from shopping on the site and more recently blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.
  • JPMorgan Chase – CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow outside agents to access accounts, calling it “too risky.”
  • Delta & Amtrak – some users report they’ve been unable to use agents to book trips from these providers.
  • Target – Muse was caught in Target’s bot check one day but got through the next; later Muse was blocked again when asked for mattress recommendations, despite being able to pull from the site minutes earlier. Target has AI shopping partnerships with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft.
  • General bot‑blocking systems can make agents inconsistent, reducing usefulness for the tasks tech companies tout as the future.

💬 Real‑world experiences

  • When asked for the best per‑piece granola‑bar price, Muse offered options from Sam’s Club, Walmart, and Costco, but noted that Amazon might have had the lowest price, yet it was “hard‑blocked” from browsing so Muse couldn’t confirm.
  • Muse suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to the user’s address while searching for the best price on granola bars.
  • On The RealReal, a subscription gives shoppers early access to new items; placing an item in the cart reserves it for 20 minutes. The author instructed Muse to bulk‑add the newest 10 listings from a favorite brand, effectively blocking other shoppers.
  • Even when they work, the agents “suggest a more annoying future for humans.”

🛒 Amazon’s own agentic feature

  • Amazon runs its own on‑platform agentic shopping feature that monitors prices, automatically reorders items, and purchases products based on rules set by human users.
  • A separate Amazon feature that uses an agent to purchase products from other sites without leaving Amazon angered smaller businesses, who say they didn’t consent to having their storefronts scraped and featured on Amazon.
  • Amazon spokesperson Maxine Tagay confirmed the company “requested that Meta remove Amazon” from Muse and stated that third‑party applications “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”

🔮 Why it matters

  • AI agents are getting blocked left and right, indicating a clash between the promise of democratized labor and the technical, legal, and business realities of e‑commerce platforms.
  • The friction observed—technical problems, frequent blocking, and unintended consequences like reserving inventory for a bot—highlights the challenges ahead for making agentic shopping a seamless part of everyday life.

#AIagents #ShoppingBots #Ecommerce #Amazon #Meta

Source: AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary

item.title: Meta pauses Muse chat-sharing feature after security leak
item.description:
Meta pauses Muse chat-sharing feature after security leak

Meta has temporarily disabled the Muse sharing feature that let users generate a public link to an AI conversation after researchers uncovered thousands of publicly discoverable links.

🔍 Overview

  • Researchers at security firm Claroc reported more than 6,800 Muse links exposed through public DNS records.
  • The exposure included sensitive data such as a marketing company’s revenue review, a small‑business loan application, a workplace full‑year staff calendar, and interview notes for an AI‑lab candidate.
  • In response, Meta paused the sharing functionality while it reviews the report.

🧩 How it works

  • Muse allowed users to “share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link,” according to spokesperson Tracy Clayton.
  • Each shared page’s URL was built from the conversation’s title, a short descriptive phrase, and a random ID.
  • The hostname often revealed the content type, and because the link contained the same title and ID, a hostname pulled from DNS could be used to reconstruct the full URL.

⚙️ Key details

  • Discovery method: Claroc searched public DNS records, which act as a directory for web traffic, to rebuild links.
  • Volume: Over 6,800 links were identified, with hundreds viewed by the researchers.
  • Sensitive examples:
    • Marketing company’s revenue review
    • Small‑business owner’s loan application
    • Workplace full‑year staff calendar
    • Notes for a job candidate’s call with an AI lab
  • Meta’s response:

    “However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.”

💡 Why it matters

  • The incident highlights how easily AI conversation links can become public when URL design leaks metadata.
  • It joins previous cases where chat exports from OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and xAI’s Grok appeared in Google Search, underscoring broader privacy challenges in AI chat sharing features.

#Meta #MuseAI #Privacy

Source: Meta pauses Muse sharing after researchers find AI chats on the web

item.title: Meta removes AI training language from commercial terms
item.description:
Meta removes AI training language from commercial terms

Meta has revised its commercial terms to strip out wording that had been read as granting the company permission to scrape content—including news sites—for AI training.

🔍 Overview

  • The update eliminates the specific clause that could be interpreted as allowing Meta to use any content from domains, web pages, or URLs for developing and training its AI products.
  • The change follows backlash from experts and content‑owners.

✍️ What changed

  • The controversial language no longer appears on the commercial terms page.
  • The removed clause previously read:

    “… Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features …”

  • Meta states that the crawling terms now apply only to its ads and business products.

🗣️ Company response

  • Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts said, “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.”
  • Roberts added in a follow‑up statement to The Verge:

    “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

📜 Expert interpretation

  • Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, professor of digital and information law at Cornell, had interpreted the original wording as an attempt to give Meta the right to scrape sites for free and to override a site’s robots.txt instructions.

⚖️ Why it matters

  • Removing the language addresses concerns that Meta could train AI models on scraped content without compensation to content owners.
  • The clarification reaffirms that standard web‑crawling behavior and robots.txt signals remain unchanged.
  • It highlights ongoing tension between large tech platforms’ AI ambitions and existing copyright and web‑scraping norms.

#Meta #AI #WebCrawling #TermsUpdate

Source: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites

item.title: Meta's Muse AI Assistant Raises Privacy Concerns Over Data Harvesting
item.description:
Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Raises Privacy Concerns Over Data Harvesting

Meta’s recently released AI personal assistant, Muse, has sparked debate regarding the collection of user and third-party data. Since its release last month, the agent has reached No. 1 on Apple’s App Store with millions of downloads, utilizing a virtual avatar to request access to sensitive information including bank accounts, passwords, contact lists, and chat logs.

🧩 How it works

Muse is designed as an autonomous helper intended to perform menial tasks such as filling out invoices and sending emails. To function, the agent ingests large amounts of personal context, which Meta states is gathered from public information and data the user chooses to share. Security researchers have discovered that the agent maintains an internal process that updates profiles of every person in a user’s life on an hourly basis.

⚙️ Key details

  • Data Scope: The agent accesses emails, messages, contacts, and photos, often including information belonging to the user’s friends and family.
  • User Interface: Critics suggest the interface uses dark patterns to encourage users to share more data than they may realize.
  • Permissions: Meta maintains that data access is opt-in. For example, the company stated that full disk access on a Mac is required for the agent to access text messages.
  • Incidents: Users have reported issues such as the exposure of a tech reviewer’s home address and the potential for the agent to access text messages, which Meta attributes to misconfigured app permissions.

💡 Why it matters

Experts from the Signal Foundation and the Electronic Frontier Foundation have raised concerns that these AI agents extend mass surveillance to sensitive data. Because the agent processes information about the user’s contacts, individuals who did not consent to using the service may still have their personal data ingested. There is currently no meaningful way for those individuals to opt out of this data collection process.

#Meta #Muse #Privacy #AIAgents #DataSecurity

Source: Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents

item.title: Meta brings Your Algorithm customization feature to Facebook
item.description:
Meta brings Your Algorithm customization feature to Facebook

Meta is introducing the “Your Algorithm” feature to Facebook, allowing users to directly manage and customize the content they see in their feed and Facebook Reels. This toolset is part of a broader implementation of AI-powered features designed to provide users with more control over their algorithmic recommendations.

🧩 How it works

  • Users can access the feature via the three dots menu on individual posts.
  • You can select “interested” or “not interested” to adjust recommendations.
  • The system may ask follow-up questions to gain more detail on user preferences.
  • You can describe in your own words what content you want to see more or less of.

⚙️ Key details

  • Recommendations respond in real time, adapting within the same session to reflect user input.
  • Meta is increasing the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in ranking systems to interpret user intent and natural language.
  • The feature has previously launched on Instagram and as “Dear Algo” on Threads.

💡 Why it matters

Meta states that using LLMs allows the algorithm to incorporate interests, context, and intent behind natural language, effectively creating an algorithm that users can talk to.

item.title: OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse
item.description:
OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman introduced Dots, a new AI agent designed to set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI. The announcement included direct critiques of Meta’s Muse, with OpenAI positioning its new assistant as a more secure and trustworthy alternative to its primary competitor.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI executives used the launch of Dots to highlight security concerns surrounding Meta’s Muse, which had previously launched as a safer alternative to the agent OpenClaw. While Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised Muse was built for privacy and security, the platform has faced scrutiny over data collection and vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s leadership, including Codex product lead Alexander Embiricos, stated the company is focused on providing the most secure assistant while avoiding the mistakes of rivals.

⚙️ Key details

AI Agent Developer Stated Privacy and Security Approach
Dots OpenAI Zero data retention policy options for enterprises and individual user-set rules.
Muse Meta User data stored in isolated Linux VMs with browser, CPU, memory, and storage.
OpenClaw (Not specified) Predecessor to Muse; described as less safe than subsequent alternatives.

🧩 Capabilities and Controls

OpenAI and Meta have implemented different strategies to manage user data and agent behavior:

item.title: AI Hallucinations Undermine Customer Service Workers' Authority
item.description:
AI Hallucinations Undermine Customer Service Workers’ Authority

Generative AI tools are increasingly causing customers to challenge the expertise of service workers, leading to dangerous situations like ignored allergy warnings and dismissed sommeliers.

🔍 Overview

A growing number of customer service workers report that patrons are trusting AI-generated information over the advice of human experts, a trend exacerbated by AI hallucinations. This phenomenon is affecting restaurants, national parks, childcare facilities, and other service industries.

🧩 How it works

Customers use generative AI tools like ChatGPT to answer questions or plan experiences. When the AI produces incorrect information — known as a hallucination — some users insist the AI is correct, even when confronted by human professionals.

Examples from the evidence include:

  • A server in New York City, Madison, has guests push back when she tells them a dish contains an allergen, saying “ChatGPT disagrees.”
  • One diner with a shellfish allergy ordered a fish dish with a shellfish-based broth because they believed ChatGPT over the server’s warning.
  • Sommeliers at a Michelin-recommended Italian restaurant are being dismissed from tables as guests prefer to ask ChatGPT for wine recommendations.
  • Customers have requested bottles that the restaurant doesn’t carry — or that don’t exist at all.

⚙️ Key details

The issue extends well beyond restaurants:

  • River rangers: Jason, a river ranger on federal lands in the Mountain West, says visitors arrive with nonsensical AI-generated itineraries that include hallucinated campsites or schedules out of geographical order. Some groups remain skeptical even when rangers explain the errors while pointing at a map.
  • Childcare professionals: Casey, an after-school program teacher in New York, reports parents and caretakers turning to ChatGPT or Claude for childhood development advice. One family insisted that ChatGPT’s recommended sleep schedule was fine, even though the child needed two to three more hours of sleep a night based on his behavior.
  • General customer service: Workers at movie theaters, coffee shops, and Apple Stores report customers asking for products or features that don’t exist.

💡 Why it matters

“Mass adoption of generative AI tools is rewriting the old adage that has long been a thorn in the side of restaurant and retail workers: ‘The customer is always right,’” according to the evidence. Now, workers must contend with customers who trust AI chatbots over human expertise.

To “soften the blow” of AI hallucinations, Madison and her colleagues soften their language, saying things like, “We have this really hyper-specific wine list, maybe it’s showing you a French wine, and we don’t carry French wine,” instead of telling the customer the AI made up a wine brand.

The launch of a new AI agent, Muse from Meta, is expected to worsen the problem, as are similar tools from other companies.

Meta Muse AI Agent Faces Multiple Security Vulnerabilities and Data Leaks

Meta’s new consumer-facing AI agent, Muse, has encountered two security disclosures in a single week, including an exploit allowing account hijacking and a leak of its root filesystem.

🔍 Security Issues

  • Filesystem Leak: Peter James and Jonny L. Saunders independently coaxed Muse into sharing its entire root filesystem, including Ubuntu system files, internal documentation, and app templates. Saunders noted that Muse had “Almost no prompt injection resistance.”
  • Account Hijacking: Security researcher Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to hijack the AI agent, redirect transcription processing, and gain complete control of a user’s Muse account. Meta issued a hotfix for this issue.

🧩 How it Works

  • Infrastructure: Muse runs in persistent Linux virtual machines for each user. Zuckerberg stated these are “isolated linux computer[s] with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.”
  • Data Handling: The agent stores its memory in plain Markdown files and performs a nightly “dream” review of recent conversations to create guidance for future interactions.
  • Capabilities: Many capabilities are hard-coded, such as the ability to cancel subscriptions and the “machinery that manages runaway agent spawning.”
  • Integrations: James found references to “Meta Home Link,” which appears to provide Muse access to devices on a home network.

⚙️ Key Details

Researchers James and Saunders gained access to JSON and Markdown files describing “Hatch” (the internal name for Muse), which detail how the system:

  • Processes requests
  • Handles data
  • Connects to services like Gmail

💡 Why it Matters

Meta representatives have responded to the filesystem leaks as follows:

Representative Perspective
Daniel Roberts (Spokesperson) Compared it to a laptop, stating “of course you can see the files” and that exporting VM data provides no privileged access to Meta infrastructure or other users’ data.
Nat Friedman (Superintelligence Labs) Tweeted that this was “intended behavior.”
David Singleton (Superintelligence Labs) Suggested users view Muse as a “free computer in the cloud” where they can do almost anything they could with a computer under their desk.

🚀 Availability

According to an Apptopia estimate, Muse has 600,000 daily active users in the US and topped the App Store charts shortly after its release.

David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs stated on X: “This was a local privilege escalation attack, not a remote exploit. Using it to do harm therefore requires malicious code already running on the user’s machine under their user account and the practical risk to users of the Muse Mac app was therefore quite low.”

  • In Jason Aten’s screenshots, Muse gave an incorrect explanation of the notification‑sync feature.

item.title: Industry Leaders and Government Clash Over AI Safety and Regulation
item.description:
Industry Leaders and Government Clash Over AI Safety and Regulation

The debate over the regulation of frontier AI has intensified as industry CEOs, researchers, and the U.S. government disagree on the existence of existential risks and the necessity of mandatory safety standards.

💡 Why it matters

There is a growing divide regarding the safety of AI development:

  • Researchers from labs including Google DeepMind and Anthropic have resigned, stating that models pose real threats and safety is not being taken seriously across the industry.
  • Some researchers believe the chance of AI killing humanity is greater than 10 percent.
  • Conversely, the Trump administration has called the idea of an AI safety crisis a “hoax,” with the president stating “The robots will not be taking over.”

⚙️ Key details

Various leaders have proposed different paths for the industry:

Entity Position or Proposal
Dario Amodei (Anthropic) Proposed a three-step plan: embedding third-party evaluators in labs, domestic industry coordination, and forging international agreements.
Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis, Elon Musk Publicly seemed to agree on aspects of Amodei’s three-step plan.
Mark Zuckerberg (Meta) Opposes limiting company autonomy, stating each lab has the responsibility to move at the pace required to train models safely.
Trump Administration Denounced a “SICK conspiracy” against AI and data centers, asserting the only needed guardrails is a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

🔍 Regulatory Conflict

Efforts to coordinate safety have met with significant resistance:

  • Zuckerberg, Musk, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang scuttled proposals for an industry-funded independent regulator similar to FINRA.
  • While some companies requested antitrust exemptions to coordinate on safety, former antitrust chief Jonathan Kanter and current officials like Lina Khan have been involved in a reboot of American antitrust policy. David Sacks has retweeted Khan stating there is no need for an antitrust exemption.
  • The Trump administration’s current stance contrasts with Executive Order 13960, which was signed during the first Trump administration to create principles for federal AI use protecting privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties.
  • Chris Lehane of OpenAI stated that government has an “important role” in ensuring AI is developed safely.

#AISafety #AIRegulation #Anthropic #OpenAI #Meta

Meta has launched Muse, its first foray into AI-powered productivity tools. The company describes the AI agent as a tool designed to “take the busywork off your plate” by assisting with tasks such as emails, trip-planning, and online shopping.

🧩 How it works

Muse operates using a cloud-based virtual computer to carry out actions. To function, the agent requires permissions to access third-party accounts; for example, connecting to a Google account allows Muse to access, read, and delete emails.

  • Content Generation: Creates images, videos, AI podcasts, and interactive documents or webpages called “artifacts”.

Feature Capability

Email Management Can delete promotional emails and updates
Subscriptions Can find and cancel forgotten subscriptions

Tests of the tool reveal varying results regarding safety and data access. Muse refused to generate images of an “Apple CEO” or specific cartoon characters, yet it successfully generated images and video of a product launch event featuring Apple’s logo and device hallucinations.

Regarding privacy, Meta states it does not share information with advertisers and only exchanges data with third-party apps that is “needed for them to work for you.” However, Muse demonstrated the ability to access API data from connected Instagram and Facebook accounts to surface specific user interests not visible in the app’s UI, and it identified a user’s current location using a shipping address from an Amazon order.

item.description:
Meta Introduces Muse Personal AI Agent for Everyday Tasks

Meta has launched Muse, a personal AI agent powered by the in-house Muse Spark model. The product is part of a multi-billion dollar strategy overhaul intended to revitalize Meta’s position in the AI race and catch up to rivals such as Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI.

🔍 Overview

Muse is described by Meta as a “personal AI agent” designed to put AI in the hands of virtually anyone. While Meta pitches it as “the world’s first personal AI agent built for everyone,” it is similar to various AI assistants and teammates offered by competitors.

🧩 How it works

Muse is designed to handle everyday tasks and projects. Its capabilities include:

  • Autonomous Action: Once given a goal, Muse can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on behalf of users.
  • Background Processing: For lengthy tasks, Muse continues working after the app is closed and returns to the user if it requires approval (such as for a purchase) or if something changes.
  • Contextual Memory: The agent remembers details shared by users, even if mentioned only once, to provide unprompted suggestions.
  • Simple Interface: Users can communicate with the assistant via the Muse app or WhatsApp.

⚙️ Key details

Meta has focused on ease of use and privacy to distinguish Muse from other tools, many of which target technically-minded individuals or businesses.

Competitor Tool Target Audience/Nature
OpenAI ChatGPT Work Businesses or technically-minded individuals
Anthropic Claude Cowork Businesses or technically-minded individuals
Microsoft Copilot Tasks Businesses or technically-minded individuals
SpaceXAI Grok Bot Businesses or technically-minded individuals

Google Gemini Spark Similar audience to Muse

Privacy and Security:

  • Data Control: Users can opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta’s AI models and can instruct Muse to “forget” specific learned information.
  • Virtual Isolation: Muse runs on a virtual computer in the cloud to keep data separate from other agents.
  • Sentinel: A separate AI agent named Sentinel patrols the virtual machine to ensure Muse cannot reach the internet without approval.
  • Payment Security: Muse has no visibility into payment method passwords and currently supports secure checkout via Stripe’s Link, with 1Password and Shop Pay support coming soon.
  • Future Encryption: Meta plans to introduce a “confidential” version of the virtual machine later this year that is encrypted so even Meta cannot access it.

🚀 Availability

  • iOS
  • Android

item.title: Meta's Instagram AI Labeling System Erroneously Tags Original and Minorly Edited Photos
item.description:
Meta’s Instagram AI Labeling System Erroneously Tags Original and Minorly Edited Photos

Instagram’s system for labeling synthetically generated content has recently gone haywire. Over the last few weeks, users have reported that Meta is automatically applying an “AI Content” label to original photos that were not created or edited with generative AI, while failing to tag actual AI images that should be labeled.

🔍 Overview

Users are reporting widespread issues with Instagram’s automatic labeling system. The visible AI labels, which are intended to help people quickly identify synthetic content at a glance, are instead being placed on original photography. This includes images with minor touch-ups, such as negligible blemish-fixing or edits made with basic design tools.

⚙️ Key Details

Several specific issues and edge cases have emerged regarding the erroneous tags:

  • Canva Integration: Content strategist Jess Bruno flagged concerns regarding Canva’s Background Remover tool. Canva explained that some of its assistive AI tools “were being tagged as generative.” While Canva claims the issue is now resolved on its end, some Threads users report that using the tool still results in their images being tagged. Conversely, other users report that none of their images edited prior to the fix were tagged, and the tool did not apply the C2PA metadata that Meta uses for detection.
  • Poisoned Content: One user discovered that Meta applied the AI tag to an image that had been “poisoned”—subtly tweaked to make it useless for AI training or to degrade AI models—while leaving an unpoisoned version of the same content untagged.
  • Brand Accounts: The cosmetics company About Face, founded by the singer Halsey, had the “AI Content” tag automatically applied to its recent Instagram photos. The brand’s social manager clarified to commenters that no AI was used to create the images.
  • Metadata Misalignment: Certain Apple Intelligence tools in iOS 27 (Spatial Reframing, Extend, and Clean Up) embed Google’s invisible SynthID watermark. Although tagged images in these recent mishaps do not have SynthID embedded, the Meta label claims it detected signals that typically identify content as “entirely AI-generated” rather than merely modified.

🧩 How it works

In February, Meta announced it would scan images for IPTC and C2PA metadata to determine with reasonable certainty whether generative AI was used to create or edit them.

In 2024, this detection system swept up pictures whose Adobe metadata indicated minor generative AI retouching, even if the final photograph was substantively unchanged. While Meta promised to tweak its approach to better reflect the amount of AI used, the latest erroneous labels do not have a clear link to generative AI usage. Outside of these mishaps, testing indicates that the label was only applied on images edited or fully generated using the Meta AI app.

item.title: Building the Open Agent Ecosystem Together: Introducing OpenEnv
item.description:
🚀 Building the Open Agent Ecosystem Together: Introducing OpenEnv

The new post-training stack developed by Meta, showing how OpenEnv integrates with libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth

With tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure. But compute is only one side of the coin. The other side is the developer community; the people and tools that make agentic systems possible. That’s why Meta and Hugging Face are partnering to launch the OpenEnv Hub: a shared and open community hub for agentic environments.

Agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else. They bring clarity, safety, and sandboxed control to agent behavior.

These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.

⚠️ The Problem

Modern AI agents can act autonomously across thousands of tasks. However, a large language model isn’t enough to get those tasks to actually run — it needs access to the right tools. Exposing millions of tools directly to a model isn’t reasonable (or safe). Instead, we need agentic environments: secure, semantically clear sandboxes that define exactly what’s required for a task, and nothing more. These environments handle the critical details:

  • Clear semantics about what a task needs
  • Sandboxed execution and safety guarantees
  • Seamless access to authenticated tools and APIs

💡 The Solution

To supercharge this next wave of agentic development, Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face are partnering to launch a Hub for Environments: a shared space where developers can build, share, and explore OpenEnv-compatible environments for both training and deployment. The figure above shows how OpenEnv fits in the new post-training stack being developed by Meta, with integrations for other libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth underway.

Starting next week, developers can:

  • Visit the new Environment Hub on Hugging Face where we will seed some initial environments
  • Interact with environments directly as a Human Agent
  • Enlist a model to solve tasks within the environment
  • Inspect which tools the environment exposes and how it defines its observations
  • Every environment uploaded to the Hub that conforms to the OpenEnv specification automatically gains this functionality — making it fast and easy to validate and iterate before running full RL training

Alongside this, we’re releasing the OpenEnv 0.1 Spec (RFC) to gather community feedback and help shape the standard.

📋 The RFCs

In the current state of the repository, environment creators can create environments using step(), reset(), close() APIs (part of RFCs below). A few examples on how to create such environments can be seen in the documentation. Environment users can play with local Docker based environments for all environments already available in the repo. Following RFCs are under review:

  • RFC 001: Establish architecture for how the core components like Environment, Agent, Task, etc. are related
  • RFC 002: Propose basic env interface, packaging, isolation and communication w/ environment
  • RFC 003: Propose encapsulation of MCP tools through environment abstraction and isolation boundaries
  • RFC 004: Extend tool support to cover unified action schema covering tool calling agents as well as CodeAct paradigm

🎯 Use Cases

The OpenEnv ecosystem enables several powerful use cases:

  • RL Post Training: Pull in environments across collections and use them to train RL agents with TRL, TorchForge+Monarch, VeRL etc.
  • Environment Creation: Build an environment and ensure that it interops with popular RL tools in the ecosystem, share with collaborators, etc.
  • Reproduction of SOTA Methods: Easily replicate methods like those from FAIR’s Code World Model by integrating environments for agentic coding and software engineering
  • Deployment: Users can create an environment, train on the same environment and then use the same for inference too (the full pipeline)

⚙️ What’s Next

This is just the beginning. We’re integrating the OpenEnv Hub with Meta’s new TorchForge RL library, and collaborating with other open-source RL projects such as verl, TRL, and SkyRL to expand compatibility. Join us at the PyTorch Conference on Oct 23 for a live demo and walkthrough of the spec, and stay tuned for our upcoming community meetup on environments, RL post-training, and agentic development.

Getting Started 🔧

👉 Explore the OpenEnv Hub on Hugging Face and start building the environments that will power the next generation of agents

👉 Check out the 0.1 spec which can be found implemented in the OpenEnv project → we welcome ideas and contributions to making it better!

👉 Engage on Discord and talk with the community about RL, environments and agentic development

👉 Try it out yourself - We created a comprehensive notebook that walks you through an end to end example and of course you can easily pip install the package via PyPI. This notebook walks you through the abstractions we’ve built, along with an example of how to use existing integrations and how to add yours - Try it out in Google Colab!

👉 Check out supporting platforms - Unsloth, TRL, Lightning.AI

Let’s build the future of open agents together, one environment at a time 🔥!

🙌 Credits

Originally posted at: https://huggingface.co/blog/openenv

🏁 Conclusion

The launch of OpenEnv represents a pivotal moment in the evolution of agentic AI systems. By providing standardized, secure, and shareable environments, this collaboration between Meta and Hugging Face addresses one of the most critical challenges in agent development: creating safe, controlled spaces where AI agents can learn and operate effectively.

The OpenEnv Hub democratizes access to high-quality training environments while maintaining the safety and isolation necessary for responsible AI development. With its RFC-driven approach and integration with leading RL libraries, OpenEnv is positioned to become the foundation for the next generation of agentic systems.

As the community begins to contribute environments and provide feedback on the specifications, we’re likely to see rapid innovation in both agent capabilities and safety measures. This collaborative approach ensures that the benefits of advanced AI agents will be accessible to researchers, developers, and organizations worldwide.
